When the angel Gabriel descended upon Muhammad (sa) for the first time and began teaching him God's message - the Quran - Muhammad reacted with total and utter shock. News of Muhammad's strange claim began to spread. Those who knew Muhammad (sa) best – his wife and closest friends – accepted him without question. They included a slave he had freed and adopted named Zaid.

Muhammad had lived among the Meccans for forty years prior to revelation. His outstanding moral personality had made him a great favourite of the town. However, news of his claim was met with derision and he was labelled a madman.

The chieftains initially made the Prophet into a figure of fun. As his message spread, their amusement replaced with something far more sinister. Muhammad was promoting the freedom of slaves, rights for the poor and had rejected the prevailing religious order. His message was attracting Mecca's weakest and slowly a small but loyal band of followers was established. These new teachings were seen by the rich as a direct challenge to their social order. How would they prosper if their slaves were given freed? How would they remain rich when they were expected to support the poor? How would they remain the most honoured if Muhammad was a prophet?

The Meccans now systematically persecuted the followers of this dangerous new faith. The Muslims were comparatively weak, poor and few. They faced regular beatings, torture and murder. Muhammad himself was attacked and publicly humiliated. Filth would be thrown upon him in the streets, rocks would shatter his home. When this did not work, Mecca's chiefs offered him enormous wealth, power and the most beautiful women in Arabia if only he would abandon his faith. He would not disobey the teachings revealed by God even if he were offered the sun and the moon, he replied.

The persecution reached its zenith during an economic boycott of all Muslims which lasted for several years. The Muslims were left poorer than ever and found themselves on the verge of starvation in the desert heat. Finally, the Meccans took pity and ended the boycott, but alas the damage was done and several of Muhammad's (sa) closest companions had already been brought to their knees – his wife Khadija and uncle Abu Talib (who had brought him up) both passed away within a month of the boycott's end.

But there was hope in the nearby city of Medina. There, Islam had been spreading steadily and those Muslims who could migrated. The chiefs of Mecca, seeing their escape, concluded enough was enough. They decided to murder Muhammad. News of their plan reached the prophet and after thirteen years of persecution he too escaped to Medina.

The Muslims may have fled their tormentors but they had been forced to leave all their wealth and property in Mecca. This meant they arrived at Medina impoverished. Moreover, the natural tendency of any nation on the mass arrival of poor immigrants is often distrust. Muhammad saw this danger and killed two birds with one stone. He linked individual Meccans with individual Medinites in a bond of brotherhood. The Medinite Muslims, to their eternal credit, embraced the situation fully and their hospitality was immense. They divided their wealth with their new brothers and friendships were immediately formed.

With the Muslims now the largest single party in Medina, their Prophet was naturally chosen as the head of the city-state. He immediately granted rights to people of all faiths; the Quranic law being revealed to him would only be compulsory upon those who chose to accept Islam. Faced with annihilation, the Prophet left Medina with 313 Muslims. Ill-equipped and outnumbered three-to-one, they met the Meccans at Badr. Relatives faced one another and Muhammad himself must have looked across the battle field and seen his paternal uncle Abbas. As a non-Muslim and resident of Mecca he would battle his own nephew.

Facing annihilation, the Muslims fought desperately for their faith, their lives and their families. The chiefs and generals of their opponents fell and the Meccans were made to turn their backs. The battle was won but the war had only begun.

Interestingly, Abbas was captured and tied with the other prisoners of war. That night, Muhammad could not sleep as he heard the groans of Abbas lying nearby. Seeing this, the Muslims loosened Abbas' ropes to ease his discomfort. When the Prophet heard of this, he said it was unjust for his family to receive advantages not offered to others. Muhammad ordered all the prisoners have their bonds loosened as Abbas' had been.

The skirmishes continued, but the Muslims survived for four years in a state of near-constant fear. Now the Meccans employed a new strategy. Having spread propaganda against the Muslims across the Arabian peninsula, they were able to unite the forces of numerous tribes into an enormous army of between 10,000 and 24,000 according to various estimates. Meanwhile, the Muslims had only 3,000 males including young boys, the old, the elderly and those unfit to fight in the whole of Medina.

The prophet consulted the Muslims as thousands marched against Medina. It was a Persian convert to Islam named Salman who suggested a tactical innovation from his homeland never before seen by the Arabs. So it was that the Meccans and their allies arrived to find Medina protected by a deep trench spanning the most vulnerable outskirts of the city. A violent siege lasted several days but the tactic of the trench proved successful and only a handful of Muslims were killed before the aggressors once more turned back.

War had been forced upon the Muslims and they were ever ready to return to peace. For example, when famine struck Mecca, Muhammad raised a fund to feed even his enemies. So, after four years of war, pressure began to mount upon the Meccans. Their allies noted how their constant rejection of the peaceful endeavours of the Muslims made it seem they did not want an end to hostilities. Moreover, the Muslim strength and numbers had increased and their enemies had not been able to defeat them. So it was that the Meccans succumbed to the pressure of their allies and agreed to enter into a peace treaty with Muhammad. The Muslims were somewhat disgruntled that the Prophet agreed to the terms of the Meccans despite being in a position of relative strength, but Muhammad valued peace above worldly power.

The treaty, initially agreed for a minimum of ten years did not last even two. In 629, the Meccans and their allies carried out an unprovoked and lethal attack on a tribe allied to the Muslims – whom the terms of the treaty had covered – named Khuzaa. The Khuzaa sent riders to Medina to inform Muhammad of events and demand the Muslims come to their aid.

The rapid progress of Islam meant the tables were now turned and Muhammad marched upon Mecca. Yet, just as vengeance was in his grasp he chose magnanimity. He announced that the Meccans would be treated peacefully, saying: “By God, you will have no punishment today and no reproof”. So the great city of Mecca fell with only a dozen or so unfortunate deaths, but otherwise no bloodshed. Moreover, Muhammad kept his word perfectly. To give just one example, Habbar, the Meccan man who had murdered the Prophet's pregnant daughter Zainab came to him and asked if he could really forgive such a person.
